food.text: Colchis, on the eastern shore of the Black Sea, was described as a land rich with gold, iron, timber and honey. It exported its resources mostly to the ancient Hellenic city-states, so honey from this corner of the Caucasus reached Greek tables.

The fertile valleys and protective slopes of the South Caucasus were home to grapevine cultivation and winemaking for at least 8000 years. Because of millennia of winemaking, wine remains entwined with Georgia's national identity.
From the 4th century AD, wine gained further importance in Georgian culture because the country became Christian. Wine and the vine took on a place in the new faith as well as in daily life.
According to tradition, Saint Nino, who preached Christianity in Kartli, bore a cross made from vine wood.

For centuries, Georgians drank, and in some areas still drink, their wine from horns, called kantsi, and from skins of their herd animals. The horns were cleaned, boiled and polished, which made a unique and durable drinking vessel.

The cook Soterides served King Nicomedes I of Bithynia, who reigned from 279 to 250 BCE. When his master was inland and pined for anchovies, Soterides simulated them from carefully carved turnips, oiled, salted and sprinkled with poppy seeds.

art.text: Urartu was an ancient kingdom centered on the Armenian highlands, and archaeologically it is noted for its large fortresses and sophisticated metalwork. It dominated the region in the 8th and 7th centuries BC, but constant warfare with Assyria, along with Cimmerian and Scythian attacks, weakened it. In 714 BC the main temple at Musasir was sacked and King Rusa I was crushingly defeated by Sargon II at Lake Urmia; he subsequently committed suicide in shame. Many Urartian ruins show evidence of destruction by fire.

The Garni Temple in Armenia is a colonnaded structure built in the Ionic order, making it the only largely preserved Hellenistic building in the former Soviet Union. It is conventionally identified as a pagan temple to the sun god Mihr, built by King Tiridates I in the first century AD.

The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus was destroyed and rebuilt many times in antiquity, with its final version destroyed in 262 AD. Worship of Artemis reportedly continued at the site until around 401 AD.

The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus was a tomb built between 353 and 351 BC for Mausolus, a satrap in the Achaemenid Persian Empire, and his sister-wife Artemisia II. Designed by the Greek architects Satyros of Paros and Pythius of Priene, it became known as one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

In 62 BC, King Antiochus I of Commagene built a tomb-sanctuary atop Mount Nemrut flanked by huge statues 8 to 9 meters high of himself, two lions, two eagles, and composite Greek and Iranian gods. The statues were once seated, with each god's name inscribed on them. At some point their heads were removed from their bodies and are now scattered across the site, and the damage to the heads, notably to the noses, suggests they were deliberately damaged in an act of iconoclasm.

In the early fourth century, when King Tiridates III adopted Christianity as Armenia's state religion, all pagan places of worship in the country were destroyed by Gregory the Illuminator. Scholars regard the Garni Temple as the only pagan, Hellenistic, or Greco-Roman (classical) structure to have survived this widespread destruction, and they continue to debate why it was exempted.

Near the Garni Gorge in Armenia stands the ancient Geghard Monastery, which is partially carved into the mountain and has existed since the fourth century AD. It lies within walking distance of the first-century Garni Temple, built as a temple to the sun god Mihr.

Around 550 BC, a grand reconstruction of the Temple of Artemis was led by the Cretan architect Chersiphron and funded by Croesus of Lydia. That version stood until 356 BC, when it was burned down by an arsonist popularly identified as Herostratus, who set fire to the wooden roof-beams seeking fame at any cost. The Ephesians sentenced him to death and forbade anyone from mentioning his name, though Theopompus later noted it. Modern scholars doubt the story, since Karwiese points out that Herostratus only divulged his purpose under torture, which does not fit a man seeking fame.

Standing about 45 meters tall, the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus had each of its four sides adorned with sculptural reliefs by a different Greek sculptor: Leochares, Bryaxis, Scopas, and Timotheus. In total the monument contained 400 freestanding sculptures.

Not all scholars agree the Garni Temple was a temple: in 1982 Richard D. Wilkinson argued the building was actually a tomb built around 175 AD for one of Armenia's Romanized kings. He based this on comparisons with Greco-Roman tombs of western Asia Minor and on nearby graves dating to about that time.

Ancient writers describe the Temple of Artemis as adorned with paintings and columns gilded with gold and silver, alongside works by renowned Greek sculptors including Polyclitus, Pheidias, Cresilas, and Phradmon. Pliny also recorded images of Amazons among its decorations, carved by the sculptor Scopas.

The 2nd-century AD writer Pausanias reported that the Temple of Artemis housed a gallery of images above an altar dedicated to Artemis Protothronia. Among them was an ancient figure of Nyx, the primordial goddess of Night, made by the sculptor Rhoecus in the 6th century BC.

war.text: Anatolia fell under Achaemenid Persian rule around 550 BC. After the Greco-Persian Wars the Aegean coast was incorporated into the Delian League in the 470s BC. Alexander the Great finally wrested control of the whole region from Persia in the 330s BC.

In 88 BC Mithridates VI Eupator, ruler of the Kingdom of Pontus, waged war on the Roman Republic to halt the advance of Roman power around the Aegean Sea. He sought to dominate Asia Minor and the Black Sea region. His hard-fought Mithridatic Wars were ultimately unsuccessful.

Galatia in central Anatolia was named after Gauls who settled there in the 3rd century BC, following the Gallic invasion of the Balkans in 279 BC. Nikomedes I of Bithynia hired 20,000 Galatian mercenaries during a struggle with his brother Zipoetes II.

The Seleucid Empire, which included Anatolia, fought a disastrous war with Rome that culminated in the battles of Thermopylae and Magnesia. The Treaty of Apamea in 188 BC forced the Seleucids to retreat from Anatolia. Rome's allies, the Kingdom of Pergamum and the Republic of Rhodes, received the former Seleucid lands there.

The last Lydian king, Croesus, invaded Persia, and the Battle of Pteria ended without a victor. Pressing deeper into Persia, he was thoroughly defeated at the Battle of Thymbra by Cyrus II in 546 BCE.

The Ionian Revolt spread across Anatolia, and with Athenian aid Aristagoras held firm for a time, despite the loss in the Battle of Ephesus. The burning of Sardis in 498 BCE enraged Darius so much that he swore revenge upon Athens. The Persian army then swept through Ionia, re-taking city by city, and the Battle of Lade outside Miletus in 494 BCE put an end to the revolt once and for all.

King Tiglath Pileser III of Assyria conquered Urartu in 745 BC. By 714 BC it was being ravaged by both Cimmerian and Assyrian raids. After 645 BC, Scythian attacks forced Urartu to become dependent on Assyria. Assyria itself then fell in 612 BC to a combined attack of Scythians, Medes and Babylonians.

After the war with Nikomedes ended in 277 BC, the Galatians slipped out of his control and began raiding Greek cities in Asia Minor. They looted Cyzikus, Ilion, Didyma, Priene, Thyatira and Laodicea on the Lycus. The citizens of Erythras paid them ransom instead.

A revolt by Naxos in 502 BCE led Aristagoras of Miletus to plan to share the island's wealth with Artaphernes, satrap of Lydia, in return for his help. When Aristagoras failed to deliver the promised rewards, the Persians were disturbed, and he resorted to persuading fellow Ionians to revolt.

Esarhaddon (680 to 669 BC) was responsible for the final destruction of Urartu. His successor Ashurbanipal then extended Assyrian influence further, placing Caria, Cilicia, Lydia and Cappadocia into vassalage.

Gyges took the Lydian throne after Candaules, the last Heraclid king, was murdered by his friend and lance-bearer Gyges. Gyges waged war against the intruding Greeks and then faced Cimmerians who began to pillage outlying cities of the kingdom. This wave of attacks led to the incorporation of the formerly independent Phrygia and its capital Gordium into Lydia, and the attacks ended for good only with the rule of Sadyattes and Alyattes, ending in 560 BCE.

Antiochus' army faced the Galatians on the plain of Sardis in the Battle of the Elephants, dated to either 275 or 269 BC. Afterwards the Celts settled in northern Phrygia, a region that eventually came to be known as Galatia.
The Assyrian king Sennacherib (705 to 681 BC) encountered a new force in Anatolia: Greeks who attempted to settle Cilicia. He drove them back.

literature.text: Anatolian languages such as Hittite and Palaic ceased to be written after the Bronze Age collapse, while Luwian and several western Anatolian languages survived into the first millennium BC. Most were gradually replaced by Koine Greek in the Hellenistic and Roman periods. The poorly attested Isaurian language may have survived in the Taurus highlands into the sixth century AD.

Around the beginning of the twelfth century BC, the Hittite imperial system collapsed during the wider Late Bronze Age collapse. Hattusa was abandoned as an imperial capital, and the central Anatolian cuneiform tradition ended.

Lycian, Lydian, Carian and Sidetic disappeared from the surviving record during the Hellenistic period. Pisidian, by contrast, remained in epigraphic use under the Roman Empire, making it one of the longest-lived securely identified Anatolian languages.

The Solymoi, a people of the mountainous interior of southwestern Anatolia, are first attested in Greek epic poetry in the Iliad. There the Lycian king Iobates sends the hero Bellerophon to fight them, and Homer describes the battle as the most difficult of Bellerophon's campaigns. Bellerophon's son Isandros is said to have been killed by Ares while fighting the Solymoi.

According to Homer's Iliad, the Phrygians took part in the Trojan War as close allies of the Trojans, fighting against the Achaeans. This links a kingdom in west-central Anatolia to the heroic world of Greek epic.

Hittite and Palaic ceased to be written after the collapse of the Bronze Age political and scribal systems. Luwian and several western Anatolian languages, however, survived into the first millennium BC.
Pisidian inscriptions are written in the Greek alphabet. They are mostly short funerary texts containing personal names and genealogical formulae.

Stories of the heroic age of Greek mythology tell of several legendary Phrygian kings. They include Gordias, whose Gordian Knot Alexander the Great would later cut, Midas, who turned whatever he touched to gold, and Mygdon, who warred with the Amazons.

Scholars disagree on when the Pisidian inscriptions were written. Kloekhorst assigns them mainly to the first and second centuries AD, while Adiego reports a proposed second- to third-century date for the corpus.

Later authors disagreed about who the Solymoi were. Herodotus linked them with the pre-Lycian inhabitants of Milyas, Strabo with the Milyans and the people of Termessos, and Pliny the Elder said the Pisidians had formerly been called Solymi.

Alexander the Great severed the Gordian Knot at Gordium in 333 BC, in the temple of Sabazios. According to a legend, possibly promulgated by Alexander's publicists, whoever untied the knot would be master of Asia.

science.text: Hipparchus, born in Nicaea in Bithynia, is considered the founder of trigonometry and is most famous for his discovery of the precession of the equinoxes. He was active as a working astronomer between 162 and 127 BC.

Apollonius of Perga, born in the Anatolian city of Perga in Pamphylia, was an ancient Greek geometer whose definitions of the ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola are still the ones used today. He is generally ranked among the greatest mathematicians of antiquity alongside Euclid and Archimedes.

In 62 BC, King Antiochus I of Commagene built a tomb-sanctuary on Mount Nemrut in Anatolia, decorated with a stone relief that recorded the arrangement of stars and planets. This astronomical carving may mark when construction on the monument began.

Strabo, a Greek geographer born in Asia Minor around 64 or 63 BC, wrote the Geographica, an encyclopedic work describing the peoples and places of the known world from Britain to Central Asia. The finished version dates to the reign of Emperor Tiberius.

On the western terrace of Mount Nemrut, a large slab shows a lion beneath an arrangement of stars and the planets Jupiter, Mercury, and Mars. Scholars have read this composition as a chart of the sky on 7 July 62 BCE.

Apollonius also worked in astronomy, proposing a hypothesis of eccentric orbits to explain the apparently irregular motion of the planets. This idea was commonly accepted as true until it was superseded during the Renaissance.

To gather material for his geographic studies, Strabo traveled widely, journeying as far as Egypt and Kush and sailing up the Nile to Philae around 25 BC. Such scholarly travel across the Mediterranean and Near East was made easier by the peace of Augustus's reign.

Hipparchus determined the Moon's orbit by carefully choosing three lunar eclipses from Babylonian records, dated 22/23 December 383 BC, 18/19 June 382 BC, and 12/13 December 382 BC. He used these to fit his eccentric model of lunar motion, a method later described by Ptolemy in the Almagest.

Apollonius addressed the prefaces of his later geometry books to a patron named Attalus, possibly Attalus II Philadelphus of Pergamon. Attalus and his brother Eumenes II were patrons of the arts who expanded the library at Pergamon into international magnificence.

politics.text: Around 550 BC, Anatolia fell under Achaemenid Persian rule. After the Greco-Persian Wars, only the Aegean coast escaped, joining the Delian League in the 470s BC. Alexander the Great finally took the whole region from Persia in the 330s BC.

Lydia was famous for the world's first coinage and immense wealth in gold. Its electrum coins date to around the 7th century BC. At its greatest extent, in the 7th century BC, the kingdom covered all of western Anatolia, with its capital at Sardis.

Anatolia came under Roman rule entirely following the Mithridatic Wars of 88 to 63 BC. Earlier, the Treaty of Apamea in 188 BC had made the Seleucids retreat from Anatolia. Rome's allies, the Kingdom of Pergamum and the Republic of Rhodes, received the former Seleucid lands.

In 585 BC, a solar eclipse struck during a battle between Lydian and Median armies, and both sides took it as an omen to end their five-year war. Nebuchadnezzar II and Syennesis of Cilicia mediated the peace. It was sealed by the marriage of Astyages, son of Cyaxares, to Aryenis, daughter of Alyattes.

In 547 BC, the Lydian king Croesus besieged and captured the Persian city of Pteria in Cappadocia and enslaved its inhabitants. Cyrus the Great marched against him, and the Battle of Pteria ended in stalemate, forcing the Lydians to retreat to Sardis. Cyrus then won at Thymbra and captured Sardis by 546 BC, making Lydia a Persian satrapy.

Cappadocia survived as a Roman-protected kingdom, and Rome controlled its succession. Ariobarzanes III was executed by the Romans for opposing their control, and his brother Ariarathes X, who succeeded him, fared little better and was executed by Mark Anthony. Archelaus, a Cappadocian nobleman, then took the throne, ruling from 38 BC.

The historical Midas is believed to be the person named Mita in Assyrian texts. An Assyrian inscription mentioning Mita, dated to 709 BC in the reign of Sargon, suggests Phrygia had offered its submission and struck a truce by then.

The first pre-Socratics lived in Ionia, on the western coast of Anatolia. The Persians conquered the towns of Ionia c. 540 BC and Persian tyrants then ruled them. The Greeks revolted in 499 BC but were ultimately defeated in 494 BC.

Archelaus of Cappadocia survived by switching his allegiance from Mark Anthony to Octavian at the Battle of Actium in 31 BC, gaining Cilicia. He later angered the emperor Tiberius by supporting a rival. Summoned to Rome, he saw Tiberius declare Cappadocia a Roman province, ending the kingdom.

Phrygia's King Midas, said to have turned objects to gold, is now mostly identified with King Mita of the Mushkis, known from Assyrian accounts. Sargon II negotiated a peace treaty with him in 709 BCE. Cimmerians then poured into Phrygia, leading to Midas's downfall and suicide in 696 BCE.

Lydia's last Heraclid king, Candaules, was murdered by his friend and lance-bearer Gyges, who took over as ruler. Gyges fought intruding Greeks while Cimmerians pillaged outlying cities. These attacks led to Phrygia and its capital Gordium being incorporated into the Lydian domain.

Scholars believe the Assyrians called the Phrygians "Mushki" because the Phrygians and the Mushki, an eastern Anatolian people, were then campaigning in a joint army against Assyria. Assyrian texts thus preserve a confusion of names for Midas's people.

After Assyria's Sennacherib drove back Greeks trying to settle Cilicia, his successor Esarhaddon destroyed Urartu. Ashurbanipal then extended Assyrian influence further, placing Caria, Cilicia, Lydia and Cappadocia into vassalage. Assyria itself fell in 612 BC to Scythians, Medes and Babylonians.
Under Diocletian's tetrarchy reform of 296 CE, Lydia was revived as the name of a separate Roman province. It was much smaller than the former satrapy, but again had its capital at Sardis.

philosophy.text: Miletus was an ancient Greek city on the western coast of Anatolia, in present day Turkey. It was the home of the Milesian school, whose thinkers included Thales, Anaximander, and Anaximenes. The city played a foundational role in the development of early Greek philosophy and science.

The early Greek philosophers known as the pre-Socratics sought explanations based on natural law rather than the actions of gods. Their work has been almost entirely lost. Knowledge of their views comes from later authors' discussions of it.

Lydian religion, the beliefs of an ancient people of Iron Age Anatolia, was centred on the fertility of nature. Little is known because the sources are largely Greek. No Lydian corpus of ritual texts like the Hittite ritual tablets has been recovered.

Pre-Socratic philosophy began in the 6th century BC with three Milesians: Thales, Anaximander, and Anaximenes. Each named a different origin, or arche, of the world. For Thales it was water, for Anaximander the apeiron (the unlimited), and for Anaximenes air.

Three more early philosophers came from nearby Ionian towns: Xenophanes, Heraclitus, and Pythagoras. Xenophanes is known for criticising the anthropomorphism of gods. Heraclitus, who was notoriously difficult to understand, is known for his maxim on impermanence, ta panta rhei.
Lydia was conquered by the Persian Achaemenid Empire in c. 547 BC, yet native Lydian traditions were not destroyed. In fact, most Lydian inscriptions were written during the period of Persian rule.

In Hittite texts, pieces of Luwian language often appear in magic rituals meant to bring rain or heal the sick. These rituals give an important role to the goddess Kamrusepa. The Luwians were an Indo-European people of Asia Minor.

A 5th or 4th century BCE Lydian inscription on a stele from Sardis called on the goddess Artimus as witness to an agreement between Sardians and the Mermnad clan. The stele was left in the city's sacred precinct so the agreement would be upheld in the future.

Tiwad was the Luwian Sun god, and the Luwians had no female sun deity like the Hittite Sun goddess of Arinna. One of his epithets was tati ("father"). The Late Luwian king Azatiwada, whose name means "Beloved of Tiwad", called him "Tiwad of the Heavens".

Many Luwian religious images survive from Melid, created by one especially pious king of the 10th century. The reliefs show the king pouring libations before a number of deities. One depicts the weather god's battle with a snake-like demon, recalling the Hittite myth of Illuyanka and the Greek myth of Typhon.

Calling gods as witnesses to an agreement was a common Anatolian practice, as seen on the Sardis stele. The Hittites deposited the treaty between Tudḫaliya IV of Hattusa and Kuruntiya of Tarḫuntašša before six different deities.

culture.text: Lydian religion centred on the fertility of nature, as was common among ancient societies that depended on farming. Yet it is only thinly documented, because most of what we know comes from Greek sources, and no Lydian collection of ritual texts like the Hittite ritual tablets has been recovered.

Religion in the ancient Near East mixed formal and informal belief. Cults of specific deities had their own priesthoods and rituals, while talismanic and apotropaic magic and belief in the evil eye existed alongside them. Early Hittite religion had traits descended from Proto-Indo-European religion, but later became more assimilated to Mesopotamian religion.
culture.source_title: Religions of the ancient Near East

culture.text: Persian conquest of Lydia in about 547 BC did not wipe out native Lydian traditions. In fact, most Lydian inscriptions were written during the period of Persian rule.
The Lycians of southwestern Anatolia developed a distinctive regional culture in Lycia. It included monumental tombs and inscriptions written in the Lycian language.

The Carians lived mainly in southwestern Anatolia and also served as merchants and mercenaries abroad. They were one of several regional peoples who developed in western and southwestern Anatolia during the first millennium BC, speaking languages of the Anatolian branch.

Sacrifices in Lydia left grim remains. Pits containing pitchers, cups, plates, knives and cooking pots have been found, holding the skeletons of dismembered puppies that were not eaten. These sacrifices, probably the remains of ritual dinners, were especially offered between about 575 and 525 BC, possibly to protect the buildings of the precinct.
The Lydians worshipped a sun-god called Tiwdas, known from a theophoric name. He corresponded to the Anatolian Sun-god Tiwadas, whose name was written in Hieroglyphic Luwian.
Hittites likewise invoked gods to guarantee treaties. The treaty between Tudḫaliya IV of Hattusa and Kuruntiya of Tarḫuntašša was deposited before six different deities.

At Sardis, the remains of the temple of Artimus date from the 3rd century BC, but the site first held only an archaic limestone altar built between about 550 and 500 BC. Since nothing stood there before, the Lydian-era sanctuary of Artimus may have been located elsewhere.

A sanctuary of the deity Kufaws, still undiscovered, is suggested by lion sculptures, a votive stela showing Kufaws and Artimus, and a marble temple model from about 540 to 530 BC. It seems to have been in use from about 550 BC to the 4th century BC. Reused pieces from it in the Late Roman period suggest it may still have functioned under Roman rule.
